claims.source: HS is a universal phenomenon observed in many eukaryotic inter-species hybrids, including examples in yeast, plants, insects, birds, and mammals (Coyne and Orr, 2004; Maheshwari and Barbash, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The Bateson–Dobzhansky–Muller incompatibility hypothesis explicates hybrid sterility as a consequence of the independent divergence of mutually interacting genes resulting in aberrant interaction of new alleles that have not been tested by natural selection.
claims.source: In time, however, the Bateson–Dobzhansky–Muller incompatibility (BDMI) hypothesis (Muller and Pontecorvo, 1942; Dobzhansky, 1951; Orr, 1996) explicated HS, and more generally any hybrid incompatibility, as a consequence of the independent divergence of mutually interacting genes resulting in aberrant interaction of the new alleles that have not been tested by natural selection.
claims.evidence: This is a description of an established hypothesis supported by citations.

claims.claim: Haldane's rule posits that if one sex of the F1 offspring of two different animal races is absent, rare, or sterile, it is the heterogametic sex (XY or ZW).
claims.source: Haldane's rule posits that if one sex of the F1 offspring of two different animal races is absent, rare, or sterile, it is the heterogametic sex (XY or ZW) (Haldane, 1922).
claims.evidence: This is a description of an established rule supported by citation.

claims.claim: Chr X plays a disproportionately large role compared to autosomes in reproductive isolation.
claims.source: Another common feature refers to the disproportionately large role of Chr X compared to that of autosomes in reproductive isolation (Presgraves, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a common feature supported by citation.

claims.claim: Interaction between selfish genomic elements causing meiotic drive and their suppressors has been implicated in some instances of reproductive isolation.
claims.source: More recently, interaction between selfish genomic elements causing meiotic drive and their suppressors has been implicated in some instances of reproductive isolation (Orr, 2005; Zhang et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Only five Drosophila HS genes have been identified to date: OdsH, JYAlpha, Ovd, agt, and Taf1.
claims.source: In studies mapping HS genes, the Drosophila group of species has been the model of choice, yet only five Drosophila HS genes, namely OdsH, JYAlpha, Ovd, agt, and Taf1, have been identified to date, none of which has a known interacting partner predicted by the BDMI hypothesis (Ting et al., 1998; Masly et al., 2006; Phadnis and Orr, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a fact supported by citations.

claims.claim: None of the five identified Drosophila HS genes has a known interacting partner predicted by the BDMI hypothesis.
claims.source: In studies mapping HS genes, the Drosophila group of species has been the model of choice, yet only five Drosophila HS genes, namely OdsH, JYAlpha, Ovd, agt, and Taf1, have been identified to date, none of which has a known interacting partner predicted by the BDMI hypothesis (Ting et al., 1998; Masly et al., 2006; Phadnis and Orr, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a fact supported by citations.

claims.claim: The first mouse HS locus Hst1 was genetically mapped in crosses of laboratory inbred strains with wild Mus musculus musculus mice.
claims.source: The first mouse HS locus Hst1 was genetically mapped in crosses of laboratory inbred strains (predominantly of Mus musculus domesticus (Mmd) origin) with wild Mus musculus musculus (Mmm) mice (Forejt and Iványi, 1974).
claims.evidence: This is a historical finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: The Hst1 locus was identified with the PR-domain-containing nine gene (Prdm9).
claims.source: Finally, we identified the Hst1 locus with the PR-domain-containing nine gene (Prdm9) (Mihola et al., 2009), which codes for histone H3 lysine 4/lysine 36 methyltransferase (Powers et al., 2016) the first and still the only HS gene known in vertebrates.
claims.evidence: This is a key finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: Prdm9 codes for histone H3 lysine 4/lysine 36 methyltransferase.
claims.source: Finally, we identified the Hst1 locus with the PR-domain-containing nine gene (Prdm9) (Mihola et al., 2009), which codes for histone H3 lysine 4/lysine 36 methyltransferase (Powers et al., 2016) the first and still the only HS gene known in vertebrates.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a fact supported by citation.

claims.claim: Most tested laboratory inbred strains share either the Prdm9Dom2 or the Prdm9Dom3 allele.
claims.source: Most of the tested laboratory inbred strains share either the Prdm9Dom2 or the Prdm9Dom3 allele (Parvanov et al., 2010; Brunschwig et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a fact supported by citations.

claims.claim: The male sterility of (PWD x C57BL/6)F1 hybrids depends on the interaction of the heterozygous allelic combination Prdm9Msc/Prdm9Dom2 with the PWD allelic form of the X-linked Hybrid sterility X Chromosome 2 locus, Hstx2Msc.
claims.source: The male sterility of (PWD x C57BL/6)F1 (henceforth PB6F1) hybrids depends on the interaction of the heterozygous allelic combination Prdm9Msc/Prdm9Dom2 with the PWD allelic form of the X-linked Hybrid sterility X Chromosome 2 locus, Hstx2Msc (Dzur-Gejdosova et al., 2012; Bhattacharyya et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a key finding supported by citations.

claims.claim: Less than 10% instead of the expected 25% of (PWD x B6) x B6 male backcross progeny replicated the infertility of male PB6F1 hybrids.
claims.source: The proper allelic combination of Prdm9 and Hstx2 genes is necessary but not sufficient to govern HS completely because less than 10% instead of the expected 25% of (PWD x B6) x B6 male backcross progeny replicated the infertility of male PB6F1 hybrids (Dzur-Gejdosova et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by citation.

claims.claim: Approximately 90% of primary spermatocytes of infertile PB6F1 hybrids have multiple unsynapsed autosomal pairs decorated by phosphorylated histone γH2AX as a mark of persisting unrepaired DNA double-strand breaks.
claims.source: We observed multiple unsynapsed autosomal pairs decorated by phosphorylated histone γH2AX as a mark of persisting unrepaired DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) in approximately 90% of primary spermatocytes of infertile PB6F1 hybrids.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claims.claim: The asynapsis in PB6F1 hybrids was accompanied by disturbed transcriptional inactivation of sex chromosomes at the first meiotic prophase.
claims.source: The asynapsis was accompanied by disturbed transcriptional inactivation of sex chromosomes at the first meiotic prophase (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is an observation supported by citations.

claims.claim: Replacement of the mouse sequence encoding the PRDM9 zinc-finger array with the orthologous human sequence reversed sterility in (PWD x B6-Prdm9Hu)F1 hybrid males.
claims.source: Recently, the role of PRDM9 zinc-finger-domain binding sites within noncoding genomic DNA has been demonstrated in PB6F1 male HS. Replacement of the mouse sequence encoding the PRDM9 zinc-finger array with the orthologous human sequence reversed sterility in (PWD x B6-Prdm9Hu)F1 hybrid males (Davies et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claims.claim: In PB6F1 hybrids, roughly 70% of the Prdm9-directed DSBs hotspots identified by the DMC1 ChIP-seq method were enriched on the 'nonself' homologous chromosome.
claims.source: In PB6F1 hybrids, roughly 70% of the Prdm9-directed DSBs hotspots identified by the DMC1 ChIP-seq method were enriched on the 'nonself' homologous chromosome, as the DSB hotspots determined by the B6 allele of Prdm9 were found predominantly on PWD chromosomes, and vice versa.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: Chromosome-specific quantification of asymmetry correlated well with the asynapsis rate across five arbitrarily chosen chromosomes of PB6F1 hybrids.
claims.source: Chromosome-specific quantification of asymmetry correlated well with the asynapsis rate across five arbitrarily chosen chromosomes of PB6F1 hybrids (Davies et al., 2016; Smagulova et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by citations.

claims.claim: One third of PRDM9-dependent DSBs were reported within sequences that have at least some repetitive character.
claims.source: Recently, one third of PRDM9-dependent DSBs were reported within sequences that have at least some repetitive character, indicating that inappropriately high DSB levels in transposons and other repetitive elements may contribute to the infertility seen in some mouse hybrids (Yamada et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claims.claim: All autosomes of PB6F1 hybrid males displayed a certain degree of asynapsis, with frequencies ranging from 2.6% (Chr 1) to 42.2% (Chr 19).
claims.source: All autosomes of hybrid males displayed a certain degree of asynapsis, classified as complete, partial, or intermingled (more than two tangled univalents within labeled chromatin cloud), with frequencies ranging from 2.6% (Chr 1) to 42.2% (Chr 19) (Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study.

claims.claim: The five smallest autosomes had higher asynapsis rates (p=5.2×10−14).
claims.source: A strong bias was evident towards higher asynapsis rates in the five smallest autosomes (p=5.2×10−14, comparison of Generalized Linear Mixed Models [GLMM], Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claims.claim: There is a strong negative correlation (Spearman's ρ=−0.760, p=0.0003) between asynapsis rate and predicted symmetric DSBs.
claims.source: Under these conditions, a strong negative correlation (Spearman's ρ=−0.760, p=0.0003) of asynapsis rate with predicted symmetric DSBs (Lange et al., 2016) can be seen (Figure 2—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claims.claim: The correlation between asynapsis rate and symmetric DSB hotspots is stronger than the correlation between asynapsis rate and chromosomal physical length.
claims.source: This correlation is stronger than the correlation of the asynapsis rate with the chromosomal physical length (Spearman's ρ=−0.681, p=0.0013).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical comparison from the study.

claims.claim: Symmetric DSBs add an additional explanation of the asynapsis rate to that provided by the chromosomal length (p=0.046).
claims.source: On the contrary, the symmetric DSBs add an additional explanation of the asynapsis rate to that provided by the chromosomal length (p=0.046, comparison of GLMM models).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claims.claim: Synapsis of a pair of homologous chromosomes depends on the presence of a certain minimum number of symmetric DSBs.
claims.source: Thus, our findings suggest that synapsis of a pair of homologous chromosomes depends on the presence of a certain minimum number of symmetric DSBs, as we elaborate further using a simulation described in the 'Discussion'.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data and modeling.

claims.claim: Subnuclear regions of asynapsed chromosomes composed of sex chromosomes and/or autosomal univalents were lacking active euchromatin in contrast to other regions of the pachytene nuclei.
claims.source: Fluorescence signal quantification revealed that subnuclear regions of asynapsed chromosomes composed of sex chromosomes and/or autosomal univalents were lacking active euchromatin in contrast to other regions of the pachytene nuclei (Figure 1—video 1).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from fluorescence microscopy.

claims.claim: The absence of active euchromatin is a consequence of the meiotic synapsis failure of intersubspecific chromosomes, known as meiotic silencing of unsynapsed chromatin (MSUC).
claims.source: We propose that the absence of active euchromatin is a consequence of the meiotic synapsis failure of intersubspecific chromosomes, known as meiotic silencing of unsynapsed chromatin (MSUC [Burgoyne et al., 2009]), which can act as an epigenetic component contributing to the meiotic phenotypes of sterile hybrids (Larson et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed interpretation supported by citations.

claims.claim: Meiotic asynapsis affects intersubspecific (PWD/B6) but not consubspecific (PWD/PWD) pairs of homologous chromosomes in sterile male hybrids.
claims.source: We have shown previously that meiotic asynapsis affects intersubspecific (PWD/B6) but not consubspecific (PWD/PWD) pairs of homologous chromosomes in sterile male hybrids from crosses of PWD females and B6.PWD-Chr # consomic males (Gregorová et al., 2008; Bhattacharyya et al., 2013, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a previous finding supported by citations.

claims.claim: All male progeny of the 2-chr crosses were fully sterile, with low testis weight and the absence of sperm in the epididymis.
claims.source: All male progeny of the 2-chr crosses were fully sterile, with low testis weight and the absence of sperm in the epididymis.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claims.claim: Introduction by recombination of 27 Mb or more of a consubspecific (PWD/PWD) interval into a pair of intersubspecific (PWD/B6) homologs effectively suppressed the asynapsis rate below the baseline of 5% in all six studied autosomes.
claims.source: Introduction by recombination of 27 Mb or more of a consubspecific (PWD/PWD) interval into a pair of intersubspecific (PWD/B6) homologs effectively suppressed the asynapsis rate below the baseline of 5% in all six studied autosomes (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claims.claim: The change point for synapsis rescue was estimated at 27.14 Mb (19.36; 34.91) (95% CI).
claims.source: The model based on the data pooled from all 2-chr crosses was selected as the best model with an estimated change point at 27.14 Mb (19.36; 34.91) (95% CI) (see Figure 3—source data 7).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claims.claim: The location of the consubspecific sequence at the telomeric end was not essential for synapsis (p=0.9573).
claims.source: In spite of the known role of subtelomeric (bouquet) association in chromosome pairing (Ishiguro et al., 2014; Scherthan et al., 2014), the location of the consubspecific sequence at the telomeric end was not essential for synapsis (p=0.9573, F-test).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claims.claim: PWD/PWD intervals of sufficient size rescued synapsis whether located at the centromeric (proximal, n = 14 cases), interstitial (n = 3), or telomeric (distal, n = 14) position.
claims.source: The PWD/PWD intervals of sufficient size rescued synapsis whether located at the centromeric (proximal, n = 14 cases), interstitial (n = 3), or telomeric (distal, n = 14) position (Figure 3—source data 1–6).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study.

claims.claim: Complete elimination of asynapsis of four of the shortest autosomes could increase the proportion of primary spermatocytes that have the full set of synapsed autosomes up to 26.7%.
claims.source: Provided that hybrid male sterility is directly dependent on chromosome synapsis, we predicted (by multiplying the probabilities of the synapsis of individual chromosomes obtained in F1 hybrids) that complete elimination of asynapsis of four of the shortest autosomes (excluding Chr 17 to avoid Prdm9PWD/PWD interference) could increase the proportion of primary spermatocytes that have the full set of synapsed autosomes up to 26.7% and could potentially abolish the apoptosis of these cells to yield around 5 million sperm cells in the epididymis of the hybrid males.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on calculations from the data.

claims.claim: In the PB6F1 cross, 100% of hybrid males displayed no sperm in the epididymis, whereas in the 4-chr cross, only 51.7% of 87 G4 males were aspermic.
claims.source: In the PB6F1 cross, 100% of hybrid males displayed no sperm in the epididymis, whereas in the 4-chr cross, only 51.7% of 87 G4 males were aspermic, 19.5% had a 0.01–0.74 × 106 sperm count, and 28.7% had 1.0–13.7 × 106 sperm cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study.

claims.claim: In the 4-chr cross, 19.5% of males had a 0.01–0.74 × 106 sperm count.
claims.source: In the PB6F1 cross, 100% of hybrid males displayed no sperm in the epididymis, whereas in the 4-chr cross, only 51.7% of 87 G4 males were aspermic, 19.5% had a 0.01–0.74 × 106 sperm count, and 28.7% had 1.0–13.7 × 106 sperm cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study.

claims.claim: In the 4-chr cross, 28.7% of males had 1.0–13.7 × 106 sperm cells.
claims.source: In the PB6F1 cross, 100% of hybrid males displayed no sperm in the epididymis, whereas in the 4-chr cross, only 51.7% of 87 G4 males were aspermic, 19.5% had a 0.01–0.74 × 106 sperm count, and 28.7% had 1.0–13.7 × 106 sperm cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study.

claims.claim: The hybrids had sperm when asynapsis was suppressed in at least three of four segregating chromosomes and when the probability of all four consomic chromosomes being synapsed was >0.7 (p=0.0014).
claims.source: As a rule of thumb, the hybrids had sperm when asynapsis was suppressed in at least three of four segregating chromosomes and when the probability of all four consomic chromosomes being synapsed was >0.7 (p=0.0014, Mann-Whitney test).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claims.claim: In PB6F1 hybrids, the observed 13.1% (11.4–14.9%) (95% CI) of fully synapsed pachynemas was double (p=0.023) the 6.6% (5.3–8.1%) rate expected by the multiplication of the observed synapsis rates of individual chromosomes.
claims.source: First, in PB6F1 hybrids, the observed 13.1% (11.4–14.9%) (95% CI) of fully synapsed pachynemas was double (p=0.023, Mann-Whitney test) the 6.6% (5.3–8.1%) rate expected by the multiplication of the observed synapsis rates of individual chromosomes (Figure 5—source data 1), indicating a trans effect of synapsed autosomes on the probability of the asynapsis of other PWD/B6 chromosome pairs.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study indicating a trans effect.

claims.claim: The asynapsis rate of nonrecombinant PWD/B6 chromosomes was dramatically reduced in 2-chr crosses or the 4-chr cross (odds ratio [OR]=0.687, p=0.0002) compared to F1 hybrid rates.
claims.source: Second, at the level of individual chromosomes, the most straightforward comparison was between the nonrecombinant PWD/B6 chromosomes, where the asynapsis rate was dramatically reduced in 2-chr crosses or the 4-chr cross (odds ratio [OR]=0.687, p=0.0002, GLMM) compared to F1 hybrid rates.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claims.claim: If the predicted synapsis rate of three chromosomes is increased by ten percent, we can expect a 4.18% (2.72–5.34%) (95% CI) decrease of asynapsis rate of the fourth chromosome (p=0.0266).
claims.source: On average, if the predicted synapsis rate of three chromosomes is increased by ten percent, we can expect a 4.18% 2.72–5.34%) (95% CI) decrease of asynapsis rate of the fourth chromosome (p=0.0266, log-log regression).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claims.claim: For chromosomes with at least 34.9 Mb of PWD/PWD segment, the trans effect could not be detected (p=0.186).
claims.source: However, for the chromosomes with at least 34.9 Mb of PWD/PWD segment (right bound of 95% CI of change point estimate), for which an additional length of PWD/PWD was not shown to affect asynapsis rate anymore, the trans effect could not be detected (p=0.186, comparison of GLMM models).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claims.claim: The genic control of HS and meiotic synapsis in PB6F1 hybrids can be demonstrated by complete restitution of fertility and meiotic pairing in males with Prdm9PWD/PWD or Prdm9PWD/B6Hu genotypes.
claims.source: The genic control of HS and meiotic synapsis in PB6F1 hybrids can be demonstrated by complete restitution of fertility and meiotic pairing in males with Prdm9PWD/PWD or Prdm9PWD/B6Hu genotypes and by partial recovery in Prdm9PWD/C3H males (Dzur-Gejdosova et al., 2012; Bhattacharyya et al., 2013; Davies et al., 2016), but a chromosome-autonomous nature of asynapsis became apparent in experiments where PB6F1 hybrids carried a single pair of PWD/PWD consubspecific homologs.
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by citations.

claims.claim: The chromosome-autonomous nature of asynapsis became apparent in experiments where PB6F1 hybrids carried a single pair of PWD/PWD consubspecific homologs.
claims.source: The genic control of HS and meiotic synapsis in PB6F1 hybrids can be demonstrated by complete restitution of fertility and meiotic pairing in males with Prdm9PWD/PWD or Prdm9PWD/B6Hu genotypes and by partial recovery in Prdm9PWD/C3H males (Dzur-Gejdosova et al., 2012; Bhattacharyya et al., 2013; Davies et al., 2016), but a chromosome-autonomous nature of asynapsis became apparent in experiments where PB6F1 hybrids carried a single pair of PWD/PWD consubspecific homologs.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claims.claim: The males with a single pair of PWD/PWD consubspecific homologs remained sterile, but the synapsis of the particular consubspecific pair was completely restored.
claims.source: The males remained sterile, but the synapsis of the particular consubspecific pair was completely restored (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: The DNA-binding zinc-finger domain of the PRDM9 molecule is responsible for sterility in PB6F1 hybrids.
claims.source: Davies et al. (2016) found that the DNA-binding zinc-finger domain of the PRDM9 molecule is responsible for sterility in PB6F1 hybrids.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claims.claim: Most PRDM9PWD-specific hotspots reside on B6 chromosomes and most of the PRDM9B6-binding sites are activated on PWD chromosomes.
claims.source: Further, they found that in the sterile hybrids, most PRDM9PWD-specific hotspots reside on B6 chromosomes and, vice versa, that most of the PRDM9B6-binding sites are activated on PWD chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claims.claim: The asymmetry of PRDM9 hotspots could be explained in part by erosion of the PRDM9-binding sites due to preferential transmission to progeny of the altered hotspots motifs.
claims.source: This asymmetry could be explained in part by erosion of the PRDM9-binding sites due to preferential transmission to progeny of the altered hotspots motifs (Boulton et al., 1997; Myers et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is an explanation supported by citations.

claims.claim: A similar pattern of higher sensitivity of smaller autosomes to the synapsis failure was observed in mice with lowered dosages of SPO11.
claims.source: A similar pattern of higher sensitivity of smaller autosomes to the synapsis failure was observed in mice with lowered dosages of SPO11 (Kauppi et al., 2013) and in the consequent two-fold DSB reduction.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claims.claim: Synaptonemal complexes nucleate at multiple recombination sites in each chromosome.
claims.source: We found that chromosomes with 27 Mb or longer stretches of consubspecific sequence always rescued full synapsis in hybrid males. The position of the consubspecific interval along the chromosome was not critical for synapsis rescue, in accordance with the finding that synaptonemal complexes nucleate at multiple recombination sites in each chromosome (Zickler and Kleckner, 2015; Finsterbusch et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Two symmetric DSBs per chromosome could be sufficient for full development of the synaptonemal complex.
claims.source: Thus, it is consistent with our data that two symmetric DSBs per chromosome could be sufficient for full development of the synaptonemal complex, as shown in Figure 6 (slope of the regression of P[asynapsis] on P[0 or one symmetric DSBs]=1.00).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on modeling and data analysis.

claims.claim: In approximately 25% of cases, a chromosome is asynapsed because there are only asymmetric DSBs and no symmetric DSBs.
claims.source: Our model predicts that in approximately 25% of cases, a chromosome is asynapsed because there are only asymmetric DSBs and no symmetric DSBs (slope of the regression of P[asynapsis] on P[0 symmetric DSBs]=4.22).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claims.claim: The trans effect refers to the enhanced probability of synapsis of a pair of intersubspecific homologs depending on successful pairing of other chromosomes in males with the Prdm9PWD/Prdm9B6, Hstx2PWD 'hybrid sterility' genotype.
claims.source: The trans effect as reported in this paper refers to the enhanced probability of synapsis of a pair of intersubspecific homologs depending on successful pairing of other chromosomes in males with the Prdm9PWD/Prdm9B6, Hstx2PWD 'hybrid sterility' genotype.
claims.evidence: This is a definition of the trans effect observed in the study.

claims.claim: PB6F1 hybrid females are fertile, obeying Haldane's rule.
claims.source: PB6F1 hybrid females are fertile, obeying Haldane's rule (Haldane, 1922) but their oogenesis is impaired, having 45% of pachynemas with one or more asynapsed autosomes.
claims.evidence: This is an observation supported by citation.

claims.claim: PB6F1 hybrid female oogenesis is impaired, having 45% of pachynemas with one or more asynapsed autosomes.
claims.source: PB6F1 hybrid females are fertile, obeying Haldane's rule (Haldane, 1922) but their oogenesis is impaired, having 45% of pachynemas with one or more asynapsed autosomes.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claims.claim: The effect of Prdm9 on asynapsis in female PB6F1 meiosis seems weak or absent.
claims.source: Nevertheless, the effect of Prdm9 on asynapsis in female PB6F1 meiosis seems weak or absent (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by citations.

claims.claim: Ninety percent of primary spermatocytes carry one or more pairs of asynapsed homologs.
claims.source: However, quantitative meiotic analyses revealed that 90% of primary spermatocytes carry one or more pairs of asynapsed homologs and, more importantly, that asynapsis is chromosome-autonomous, depending on inter-homolog (cis-) interactions (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by citations.

claims.claim: Asynapsis is chromosome-autonomous, depending on inter-homolog (cis-) interactions.
claims.source: However, quantitative meiotic analyses revealed that 90% of primary spermatocytes carry one or more pairs of asynapsed homologs and, more importantly, that asynapsis is chromosome-autonomous, depending on inter-homolog (cis-) interactions (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by citations.

claims.claim: By deliberately manipulating the synapsis of homologous chromosomes, we could modify the extent of meiotic arrest in intersubspecific PB6F1 hybrids in a predictable way.
claims.source: The findings described in this paper provide the first direct link between Prdm9-controlled asynapsis and meiotic arrest in PB6F1 male hybrids. We showed that by deliberately manipulating the synapsis of homologous chromosomes, we could modify the extent of meiotic arrest in intersubspecific PB6F1 hybrids in a predictable way.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study.

claims.claim: A particular chromosome fails to synapse in as few as 2% and maximally in 45% of PB6F1 pachynemas.
claims.source: A particular chromosome fails to synapse in as few as 2% and maximally in 45% of PB6F1 pachynemas.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claims.claim: The B6 allele of the X-linked Hstx2 locus dramatically increases the pairing efficiency but causes only a small change, if any alteration, in the profile of asymmetric hotspots.
claims.source: Oddly, the B6 allele of the X-linked Hstx2 locus dramatically increases the pairing efficiency but causes only a small change, if any alteration, in the profile of asymmetric hotspots (Davies et al., 2016; Smagulova et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by citations.

claims.claim: The mechanisms that safeguard recombination between homologous allelic sequences could function as checkpoints that disable recombination after homologous sequences have diverged sufficiently during the isolation of closely related taxa.
claims.source: It is tempting to speculate that the mechanisms that safeguard recombination between homologous allelic sequences could function as checkpoints that disable recombination after homologous sequences have diverged sufficiently during the isolation of closely related taxa.
claims.evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claims.claim: The role of the mismatch repair system in reproductive isolation has been reported in Saccharomyces species.
claims.source: Among eukaryotes, the role of the mismatch repair system in reproductive isolation has been reported in Saccharomyces species (Hunter et al., 1996; Greig et al., 2003; Liti et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cited studies.

claims.claim: Antirecombination machinery could be a means to gradually restrict gene flow between related taxa, a 'cause in fact' of speciation.
claims.source: An exciting possibility, which is experimentally testable, posits an antirecombination machinery as a means to gradually restrict gene flow between related taxa, a 'cause in fact' of speciation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a speculative possibility.

claims.claim: The PWD/Ph inbred strain originated from a single pair of wild mice of the Mus musculus musculus subspecies trapped in 1972 in Central Bohemia, Czech Republic.
claims.source: The PWD/Ph inbred strain originated from a single pair of wild mice of the Mus musculus musculus subspecies trapped in 1972 in Central Bohemia, Czech Republic (Gregorová and Forejt, 2000).
claims.evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation.

claims.claim: The C57BL/6J (B6) inbred strain was purchased from The Jackson Laboratory.
claims.source: The C57BL/6J (B6) inbred strain was purchased from The Jackson Laboratory.

results.result: Smaller chromosomes in PB6F1 hybrids exhibit higher asynapsis rates, which correlate more strongly with predicted symmetric DSB hotspots than with chromosomal length. The five smallest autosomes showed significantly higher asynapsis rates (p=5.2×10⁻¹⁴), and asynapsis rate correlated negatively with predicted symmetric DSBs (Spearman's ρ=−0.760, p=0.0003). Symmetric DSBs provide additional explanatory power beyond chromosomal length (p=0.046).
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34, C91-C92 provide converging statistical evidence from GLMM models and correlation analyses. The large sample size (4168 pachynemas from 40 males, C78) and multiple statistical tests support the conclusion. The correlation analysis appropriately compares competing explanatory variables (chromosome length vs. symmetric DSBs), and the finding that symmetric DSBs add explanatory power beyond length is statistically significant.

results.result: Introduction of 27 Mb or more of consubspecific (PWD/PWD) sequence into intersubspecific (PWD/B6) chromosome pairs effectively restores synapsis below 5% asynapsis rate in all six studied autosomes. The change point was estimated at 27.14 Mb (95% CI: 19.36-34.91), and the position of the consubspecific interval (centromeric, interstitial, or telomeric) was not critical for synapsis rescue (p=0.9573).
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 are supported by extensive experimental data from 2-chr crosses examining 122 chromosomes from over 12,000 pachynemas (C79). The segmented regression model provides a quantitative estimate with confidence intervals (C40), and the statistical test for position independence (C41) is appropriate. The finding is replicated across six different chromosomes with consistent results.

results.result: Targeted suppression of asynapsis in four of the most asynapsis-prone chromosomes partially reversed hybrid sterility. In the 4-chr cross, only 51.7% of males were aspermic compared to 100% in PB6F1 controls, with 19.5% showing low sperm counts and 28.7% showing substantial sperm counts (1.0-13.7×10⁶). Sperm presence correlated with synapsis rescue when at least three of four chromosomes were synapsed and probability of all four synapsing exceeded 0.7 (p=0.0014).
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47, C83-C84, C95 provide direct experimental evidence linking chromosome synapsis to fertility rescue. The large sample size (87 G4 males, over 6500 pachynemas analyzed, C80) and clear quantitative relationship between synapsis probability and sperm presence support the causal link. The statistical significance (p=0.0014) and correspondence between predicted and observed outcomes strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: A trans effect modulates asynapsis rates, whereby successful synapsis of some chromosomes enhances synapsis probability of other intersubspecific chromosome pairs. In PB6F1 hybrids, observed fully synapsed pachynemas (13.1%) were double the expected rate (6.6%, p=0.023). Asynapsis rates of nonrecombinant PWD/B6 chromosomes were reduced in 2-chr and 4-chr crosses (OR=0.687, p=0.0002). A 10% increase in synapsis rate of three chromosomes predicts a 4.18% decrease in asynapsis of the fourth chromosome (p=0.0266).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51, C62 demonstrate a trans effect through multiple lines of evidence: comparison of observed vs. expected synapsis rates, analysis of nonrecombinant chromosomes across different crosses, and quantitative modeling of inter-chromosome effects. The statistical tests are appropriate (Mann-Whitney, GLMM), and the effect is detected consistently across different experimental designs. However, the mechanism remains unexplained, which is acknowledged in the discussion.

results.result: Modeling based on DSB distribution predicts that two or more symmetric DSBs per chromosome are sufficient for successful synapsis. The model estimates that approximately 25% of asynapsis cases occur when there are zero symmetric DSBs, with the remaining 75% occurring with one symmetric DSB. The model assumes ~250 DSBs per cell, 0.28 proportion of symmetric hotspots, and similar DSB densities between B6 and PB6F1 males.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61, C88-C90 present a computational model with several critical assumptions. While the model is consistent with the data (slope of regression P[asynapsis] on P[0 or 1 symmetric DSBs]=1.00), the assumptions are not all directly validated: (1) C90 assumes similar DSB densities between B6 and PB6F1, which is stated as an assumption rather than demonstrated; (2) C89 assumes constant 0.28 proportion across all autosomes, which may not hold; (3) the model is based on 100,000 simulations but lacks validation against independent data. The prediction requires experimental verification.

results.result: Prdm9 causes chromosome asynapsis and infertility in PB6F1 male hybrids through a chromosome-autonomous mechanism. Approximately 90% of primary spermatocytes exhibit one or more pairs of asynapsed homologs with persistent unrepaired DSBs marked by γH2AX. The study demonstrates that deliberate manipulation of chromosome synapsis can predictably modify the extent of meiotic arrest.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3, C23, C66-C68 establish the link between Prdm9-mediated asynapsis and sterility. The high frequency of asynapsis (90%) and its chromosome-autonomous nature are supported by extensive cytological analysis. The causal relationship is strengthened by the fertility rescue experiments (C44-C47) showing that reducing asynapsis restores fertility. The γH2AX marking provides molecular evidence for unrepaired DSBs.

results.result: Asynapsed chromosomes in PB6F1 hybrids lack active euchromatin and are embedded in transcriptionally silenced chromatin, visualized by absence of extra-coding RNA (ecRNA) detected by Cot1 RNA FISH. This is proposed to represent meiotic silencing of unsynapsed chromatin (MSUC), which may contribute to the meiotic phenotype of sterile hybrids.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36, C93-C94 are supported by fluorescence microscopy and RNA FISH data (Figure 1). The observation of transcriptional silencing in asynapsed regions is consistent with known MSUC mechanisms. However, C36 is stated as a proposal rather than definitively proven causation. The interpretation is reasonable and supported by citations, but the specific contribution of MSUC to the sterility phenotype is not quantified.

results.result: In PB6F1 hybrids, approximately 70% of Prdm9-directed DSB hotspots are asymmetric, with PRDM9PWD hotspots predominantly on B6 chromosomes and vice versa. The DNA-binding zinc-finger domain of PRDM9 is responsible for sterility, and the asymmetry may be explained by erosion of PRDM9-binding sites through preferential transmission of altered hotspot motifs.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27, C55-C57 are primarily based on cited work (Davies et al., 2016; Smagulova et al., 2016) rather than new data from this study. The current study validates the correlation between asymmetry and asynapsis across chromosomes (C27). The mechanistic explanation for hotspot asymmetry (C57) is speculative but supported by literature citations. These findings provide important context for interpreting the current results.

results.result: Prdm9-independent 'default' hotspots are enriched in Chr X, and their percentage in autosomes correlates with asynapsis rate in F1 hybrids (Spearman's ρ=0.69, p=0.0012). These hotspots may represent late-forming DSBs on unsynapsed chromosomes and could be a consequence rather than cause of asynapsis.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 present a correlation analysis with significant statistical support. However, C87 explicitly acknowledges this is an interpretation ('may represent') rather than demonstrated causation. The correlation is notable but the directionality (consequence vs. cause) requires further experimental validation. The interpretation is reasonable and supported by citation to Kauppi et al. (2013).

results.result: Meiotic asynapsis affects intersubspecific (PWD/B6) but not consubspecific (PWD/PWD) chromosome pairs in sterile male hybrids. In 2-chr crosses, all male progeny were fully sterile with low testis weight and absence of sperm. Nonrecombinant PWD/PWD bivalents were always fully synapsed, while nonrecombinant PWD/B6 pairs showed highest asynapsis frequencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38, C81-C82 establish the fundamental observation that drives the experimental design. C37 is supported by previous citations, while C38, C81-C82 are direct observations from the current study. The consistent synapsis of PWD/PWD pairs and asynapsis of PWD/B6 pairs across all experiments provides strong evidence for the chromosome-autonomous nature of the effect.

results.result: PB6F1 hybrid females are fertile, obeying Haldane's rule, but their oogenesis is impaired with 45% of pachynemas showing one or more asynapsed autosomes. The effect of Prdm9 on asynapsis in female PB6F1 meiosis appears weak or absent.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65 describe sex-specific differences in the hybrid sterility phenotype. The observations are supported by data and citations. The finding that females are fertile despite substantial asynapsis (45%) contrasts with male sterility and supports Haldane's rule. However, the mechanism underlying the sex difference is not explored in detail.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that impaired recombination between evolutionarily diverged chromosomes could function as a mechanism of hybrid sterility in various sexually reproducing species. They speculate that mechanisms safeguarding recombination between homologous sequences could act as checkpoints disabling recombination after sufficient divergence, potentially serving as a gradual means to restrict gene flow between related taxa.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C71-C73 are explicitly stated as hypotheses and speculation. While the mouse data provide support for this mechanism in one system, extrapolation to 'various sexually reproducing species' requires additional evidence. C72 cites work in Saccharomyces as precedent, but broader validation is needed. These are reasonable hypotheses for future testing but are not demonstrated by the current work.

results.result: Background knowledge and prior findings establish the context for the study, including: Prdm9 as the only known vertebrate hybrid-sterility gene; its role in determining DSB sites and recombination hotspots; the genetic basis of PB6F1 hybrid sterility involving Prdm9 and Hstx2 alleles; and various observations from previous studies on hybrid sterility mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C4-C5, C9-C22, C24-C25, C28, C52, C54, C58-C59, C70, C74-C76 represent established knowledge and prior findings that are appropriately cited. These provide essential context but are not new results from this study. The citations appear accurate and the background is well-established in the literature.

results.result: The authors predicted that complete elimination of asynapsis in four of the shortest autosomes could increase the proportion of primary spermatocytes with fully synapsed autosomes to 26.7% and potentially yield around 5 million sperm cells in hybrid male epididymis.
results.evaluation: Claim C43 represents a prediction based on multiplication of individual chromosome synapsis probabilities. The subsequent experimental results (C44-C46) partially validate this prediction, though the observed outcomes show more variability than the simple multiplicative model suggests. The prediction was useful for experimental design but the actual results revealed additional complexity (trans effects).

results.result: Methodological details: males were analyzed at 60-70 days of age; 4168 pachynemas from 40 PB6F1 males were analyzed; 122 chromosomes from over 12,000 pachynemas were examined in 2-chr crosses; over 6500 pachynemas were analyzed in the 4-chr cross.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C80 provide essential methodological information and sample sizes. These are straightforward factual statements about the experimental design. The large sample sizes (thousands of pachynemas) provide adequate statistical power for the analyses performed.
